title: Angles & Parallel Lines
coreInsight: An angle measures turn or separation between rays, and intersections and parallel lines create dependable angle relationships.
narrativeTransition: Rotate a ray and track the turn before introducing named angle relationships; then use line structure rather than visual appearance to infer missing angles.
commonMisconceptions: Angle size depends on ray length.
The drawing's appearance overrides stated relationships.
Parallel-line angle rules apply even when lines are not parallel.
Vertical and supplementary angle relationships are interchangeable.

title: Triangles
coreInsight: Triangle side and angle constraints are linked, and special triangles gain additional consequences from equality and symmetry.
narrativeTransition: Move a triangle's vertex while tracking angle sum and equal-side/equal-angle relationships so the constraints become visible rather than memorized.
commonMisconceptions: A shape that is rotated or visually unfamiliar may stop 'looking' isosceles even when its defining properties hold.
Equal sides and equal opposite angles are unrelated facts.
Triangle angle sum can be used without identifying the relevant triangle.
Exterior and interior angles are interchangeable.

title: Perimeter & Area
coreInsight: Perimeter measures boundary length while area measures two-dimensional coverage, and area formulas arise from composing or rearranging simpler regions.
narrativeTransition: Trace the boundary of a shape and then tile its interior with unit squares so the two measurements are experienced as fundamentally different.
commonMisconceptions: Equal perimeter implies equal area.
Area and perimeter formulas can be swapped.
The height in an area formula must be a visible side of the shape.
Square units are optional notation rather than part of the quantity.

title: Area Decomposition
coreInsight: Area is additive and preserved under valid cut-and-rearrange operations, so complicated figures can be replaced by simpler equivalent pieces.
narrativeTransition: Give a shape with no convenient memorized formula and let the learner cut, subtract, or rearrange it into regions they already know how to measure.
commonMisconceptions: Pieces may overlap or leave gaps without changing the total.
Regions that look congruent are automatically congruent.
Removed regions should sometimes be added rather than subtracted.
Equal-looking regions are necessarily equal in area.

title: Right Triangles & Pythagorean Theorem
coreInsight: In a right triangle, the areas of squares on the legs combine to equal the area of the square on the hypotenuse, yielding a^2 + b^2 = c^2.
narrativeTransition: Build squares on all three sides of a right triangle and compare their areas before compressing the visual relationship into the theorem.
commonMisconceptions: The Pythagorean theorem applies to every triangle.
The hypotenuse is the visually longest-looking side rather than the side opposite the right angle.
After finding c^2 the square root step can be omitted.
The theorem is a distance formula with no area meaning.

title: Similarity & Scale Factors
coreInsight: Similar figures preserve shape and corresponding angles while every corresponding length scales by one factor; areas therefore scale by the square of that factor.
narrativeTransition: Take the multiplicative scaling the learner knows from ratios and apply it simultaneously to every length of a shape while keeping its angles fixed.
commonMisconceptions: Scaling is additive rather than multiplicative.
Corresponding sides can be paired arbitrarily.
Area scales by the same factor as length.
Similarity and congruence are the same relation.

title: Quadrilaterals & Polygons
coreInsight: Polygons belong to nested families defined by properties, and their angle structure can often be understood by decomposing them into triangles.
narrativeTransition: Morph quadrilaterals while tracking which properties remain true, then triangulate polygons to make angle-sum structure visible.
commonMisconceptions: Shape categories are mutually exclusive, so a square is not also a rectangle.
A polygon's name determines properties not stated or implied.
A regular polygon is just any many-sided polygon.
Interior and exterior angles can be mixed without defining the turn.

title: Circles, Arcs & Sectors
coreInsight: The radius controls a circle's metric structure; circumference and area scale differently, while arcs and sectors represent fractions determined by central angle.
narrativeTransition: Unwrap circumference and partition a circle by central angles so formulas and sector fractions emerge from geometry rather than as isolated facts.
commonMisconceptions: Radius and diameter can be interchanged.
Circumference and area are the same type of measurement.
A sector fraction depends on the radius rather than the central angle fraction.
Doubling radius merely doubles area.

title: Transformations & Symmetry
coreInsight: Transformations reveal what changes and what remains invariant; rigid motions preserve distance and angle, while dilation changes scale in a controlled way.
narrativeTransition: Move the same figure by translation, rotation, reflection, and dilation instead of redrawing separate copies, then ask which properties survived each motion.
commonMisconceptions: Rotated or reflected copies count as different shapes.
A line of symmetry can be guessed by appearance without testing correspondence.
Reflection and rotation preserve orientation in the same way.
Dilation is a rigid motion.

title: 3D Geometry
coreInsight: Volume measures three-dimensional filling while surface area measures exposed two-dimensional boundary, and both can be built from simpler layers or faces.
narrativeTransition: Extrude a familiar 2D region into layers so area becomes volume, then separately expose the outer faces to distinguish surface area.
commonMisconceptions: Surface area and volume are interchangeable measurements.
Internal or covered faces should be counted as exposed.
Linear scale, area scale, and volume scale use the same factor.
Square and cubic units can be used interchangeably.

title: Nets & Spatial Visualization
coreInsight: A two-dimensional net can encode a three-dimensional solid's adjacency and orientation, and mental folding is a transformation problem.
narrativeTransition: Cut a solid open into a net and then reverse the motion, tracking faces as they rotate into 3D positions.
commonMisconceptions: Squares that are close in a net must be adjacent after folding.
Opposite faces can be identified from flat distance alone.
Orientation is preserved without mental rotation.
Two rotated versions of the same net represent different solids.
